In SCOPe, ferritins, ribonucleotide-reductase (RNR R2)-like proteins and manganese catalases sit in the same class (a, all-alpha), the same fold (a.25, Ferritin-like) and the same superfamily (a.25.1, Ferritin-like). They are in separate families: Ferritin (a.25.1.1, which includes bacterioferritin and Dps-like ferritins), Ribonucleotide reductase-like (a.25.1.2, which also holds diiron enzymes such as the methane monooxygenase hydroxylase and acyl-ACP desaturase) and Manganese catalase (a.25.1.3). I am quoting these a.25.1.x family numbers from memory, so check them against the release in use.

The superfamily level is the key point. SCOPe puts proteins in one superfamily when structure plus supporting features (here the conserved four-helix bundle core and the dinuclear carboxylate/histidine-bridged metal site, with Glu-x-x-His motifs) indicate a probable common evolutionary origin. This holds even though sequence identity is low and the chemistry differs. So the right reading is divergent evolution from a shared dinuclear metal-binding helical-bundle ancestor, not convergence. Family boundaries mark the stronger, clearer relationships (close sequence or function), and these three families are the more distant, functionally diverged branches.

The chemistry has diverged on top of the shared scaffold:
- Ferritin uses a diiron ferroxidase centre to oxidise Fe(II) with O2 or H2O2 for iron storage and mineralisation in a 24-mer shell.
- RNR R2 uses a diiron centre to activate O2 and make a stable tyrosyl radical, which starts nucleotide reduction in the partner R1 subunit.
- Mn catalase uses a dimanganese centre to disproportionate H2O2 to O2 and water, cycling between Mn(II)2 and Mn(III)2.
- Related RNR-like enzymes such as MMO perform oxygen-atom insertion.

The metal ion, redox cycling, oligomeric assembly and partner proteins all differ between these families.

Limits on interpretation:
- Same superfamily means shared ancestry and a shared fold. It does not mean the same function, mechanism, metal specificity or substrate.
- Do not transfer function between the families. A ferritin-like fold cannot show that a protein is a catalase, an RNR subunit or an iron-storage protein.
- Function assignment needs family-level matches, conservation of the ligand residues and second-shell residues, metal identity and occupancy, quaternary structure and partner proteins, and biochemical evidence.
- Do not treat the superfamily as a single enzyme family. Within it the metal site is re-used for storage, radical generation, hydroxylation and peroxide decomposition.
- Mn catalase is not related to the haem catalases, which have a different fold and are classified elsewhere in SCOPe. Sharing the name 'catalase' does not imply homology.
- Template modelling across families is reliable for the helical core only. Loops, the active-site geometry, the metal ligands and the oligomeric interfaces can differ.
- Fold identity alone is not enough to infer ancestry. Here the case rests on the superfamily assignment plus the conserved metal-binding motif.
